vsm2.17:58.1: 58. This, firstly, is the brief treatment. The following method, however, is in detail.
vsm2.17:58.2:
(I) IGNORANCE

According to the Suttanta method ignorance is unknowing about the four instances beginning with suffering.
vsm2.17:58.3:
According to the Abhidhamma method it is unknowing about the eight instances that is to say,
the above-mentioned four together with the four beginning with the past;
vsm2.17:58.4:
for this is said: “Herein, what is ignorance? It is unknowing about suffering, unknowing about the origin of suffering,
unknowing about the cessation of suffering, unknowing about the way leading to the cessation of suffering,
vsm2.17:58.5:
unknowing about the past, unknowing about the future, unknowing about the past and future,
unknowing about specific conditionality and conditionally-arisen states” (cf. Dhs §1162).
vsm2.17:59.1: 59. Herein, while ignorance about any instance that is not the two supra-mundane truths can also arise as object (see §102),
vsm2.17:59.2: nevertheless here it is only intended subjectively as concealment.
vsm2.17:59.3: For when thus arisen it keeps the truth of suffering concealed,
vsm2.17:59.4: preventing penetration of the true individual function and characteristic of that truth.
vsm2.17:59.5: Likewise, origin, cessation, and the path,
vsm2.17:59.6: bygone five aggregates called the past, coming five aggregates called the future,
vsm2.17:59.7:
both of these together called the past and future, and both specific conditionality and conditionally-arisen
states together called specific conditionality and conditionally-arisen states—
vsm2.17:59.8: all of which it keeps concealed,
vsm2.17:59.9: preventing their true individual functions and characteristics being penetrated thus: “This is ignorance, these are formations.”
vsm2.17:59.10: That is why it is said, “It is unknowing about suffering … unknowing about specific conditionality and conditionally-arisen states.”
vsm2.17:60.3: then the formation of demerit consisting of the twelve unprofitable volitions that occur in killing living things, etc.;
vsm2.17:60.4:
then the formation of the imperturbable consisting in the four profitable volitions
associated with the immaterial sphere, which occur in development of those meditations.
vsm2.17:61.1:
61. As regards the other three, the bodily formation is bodily volition, the verbal formation
is verbal volition, and the mental formation is mental volition.
vsm2.17:61.2:
This triad is mentioned in order to show that at the moment of the accumulation of the kamma
the formations of merit, etc., occur in these three kamma doors.
vsm2.17:61.3:
For the eight sense-sphere profitable and twelve unprofitable volitions, making twenty,
are the bodily formation when they occur in the body door and produce bodily intimation.
vsm2.17:61.4: Those same volitions are called the verbal formation when they occur in the speech door and produce verbal intimation.
vsm2.17:61.5:
But volition connected with direct-knowledge is not included here in these two cases because
it is not a condition for resultant rebirth-linking consciousness later.
vsm2.17:61.6: And like direct-knowledge volition, so also volition connected with agitation is not included;
vsm2.17:61.7:
therefore that too should not be included as a condition for rebirth-linking consciousness.
However, all these have ignorance as their condition.
vsm2.17:61.8:
And all the twenty-nine volitions are the mental formation when they arise in the mind
door without originating either kind of intimation.
vsm2.17:61.9:
So this triad comes within the first triad, and accordingly, as far as the meaning is concerned,
ignorance can be understood as condition simply for formations of merit and so on.
vsm2.17:62.1:
62. Herein, it might be asked: How can it be known that these formations have ignorance
as their condition?—By the fact that they exist when ignorance exists.
vsm2.17:62.2: For when unknowing—in other words, ignorance—of suffering, etc., is unabandoned in a man,
vsm2.17:62.3:
owing firstly to his unknowing about suffering and about the past, etc., then he
believes the suffering of the round of rebirths to be pleasant
vsm2.17:62.4: and he embarks upon the three kinds of formations which are the cause of that very suffering.
vsm2.17:62.5:
Owing to his unknowing about suffering’s origin he embarks upon formations that, being subordinated to craving,
are actually the cause of suffering, imagining them to be the cause of pleasure.
vsm2.17:62.6:
And owing to his unknowing about cessation and the path, he misperceives the cessation of suffering to be in some
particular destiny such as the Brahmā-world that is not in fact cessation;
vsm2.17:62.7:
he misperceives the path to cessation, believing it to consist in sacrifices,
mortification for immortality, etc., which are not in fact the path to cessation;
vsm2.17:62.8:
and so while aspiring to the cessation of suffering, he embarks upon the three
kinds of formations in the form of sacrifices, mortification for immortality, and so on.
vsm2.17:63.1: 63. Furthermore, his non-abandonment of that ignorance about the four truths in particular
vsm2.17:63.2:
prevents him from recognizing as suffering the kind of suffering called the fruit of merit,
which is fraught with the many dangers beginning with birth, ageing, disease and death,
vsm2.17:63.3:
and so he embarks upon the formation of merit classed as bodily, verbal, and mental formations, in order to attain
that kind of suffering, like one desiring celestial nymphs who jumps over a cliff.
vsm2.17:63.4:
Also, not seeing how that fruit of merit reckoned as pleasure eventually breeds great distress
owing to the suffering in its change and that it gives little satisfaction,
vsm2.17:63.5: he embarks upon the formation of merit of the kinds already stated, which is the condition for that very suffering in change,
vsm2.17:63.6: like a moth that falls into a lamp’s flame, and like the man who wants the drop of honey and licks the honey-smeared knife-edge.
vsm2.17:63.7:
Also, not seeing the danger in the indulgence of sense desires, etc., with its results,
wrongly perceiving pleasure and overcome by defilements,
vsm2.17:63.8:
he embarks upon the formation of demerit that occurs in the three doors of kamma, like a child
who plays with filth, and like a man who wants to die and eats poison.
vsm2.17:63.9:
Also, unaware of the suffering due to formations and the suffering-in-change inherent in kamma-results in the immaterial
sphere, owing to the perversion of wrongly perceiving them as eternal, etc.,
vsm2.17:63.10:
he embarks upon the formation of the imperturbable which is a mental formation,
like one who has lost his way and takes the road to a goblin city.
vsm2.17:64.1:
64. So formations exist only when ignorance exists, not when it does not; and that is how it
can be known that these formations have ignorance as their condition.
vsm2.17:64.2:
This is said too: “Not knowing, bhikkhus, in ignorance, he forms the formation of merit,
forms the formation of demerit, forms the formation of the imperturbable.
vsm2.17:64.3:
As soon as a bhikkhu’s ignorance is abandoned and clear vision arisen, bhikkhus, with the fading
away of ignorance and the arising of clear vision he does not form even formations of merit” (cf. S II 82).
vsm2.17:65.2:
65. Here it might be asked: “Let us then firstly agree that ignorance is a condition for formations. But it
must now be stated for which formations, and in which way it is a condition.”
vsm2.17:65.3: Here is the reply: “Twenty-four conditions have been stated by the Blessed One as follows.”
vsm2.17:66.1: 66. “(1) Root-cause condition, (2) object condition, (3) predominance condition, (4) proximity condition,
vsm2.17:66.2: (5) contiguity condition, (6) conascence condition, (7) mutuality condition, (8) support condition,
vsm2.17:66.3: (9) decisive-support condition, (10) prenascence condition, (11) postnascence condition, (12) repetition condition,
vsm2.17:66.4: (13) kamma condition, (14) kamma-result condition, (15) nutriment condition, (16) faculty condition,
vsm2.17:66.5: (17) jhāna condition, (18) path condition, (19) association condition, (20) dissociation condition,
vsm2.17:66.6: (21) presence condition, (22) absence condition, (23) disappearance condition, (24) non-disappearance condition” (Paṭṭh I 1).
vsm2.17:67.1: 67. (1) Herein, it is a root-cause and a condition, thus it is root-cause condition.
vsm2.17:67.2: It is by its being a root-cause that it is a condition; what is meant is that it is a condition owing to its status as root-cause.
vsm2.17:67.3: The same method applies in the case of object condition and the rest.
vsm2.17:67.4: Herein, “cause” (hetu) is a term for a part of a syllogism, for a reason, and for a root.
vsm2.17:67.5:
For with the words “proposition” (paṭiññā), “cause” (hetu = middle term), etc., in the world
it is a member of a syllogism (vacanāvayava) that is called a cause.
vsm2.17:67.6: But in the Dispensation, in such passages as “Those states that are produced from a cause” (Vin I 40), it is a reason (kāraṇa);
vsm2.17:67.7:
and in such passages as “Three profitable root- causes, three unprofitable root-causes” (Dhs §1053),
it is a root (mūla) that is called a cause. The last is intended here.
vsm2.17:68.1:
As to “condition” (paccaya), the word-meaning here is this: It the fruit comes from that, depending
thereon (paṭicca etasmā eti), thus that is a condition;
vsm2.17:68.2: (paccaya, see note 2) the meaning is, a state occurs by not dispensing with that.
vsm2.17:68.3: What is meant is: when a state is indispensable to another state’s presence or arising, the former is a condition for the latter.
vsm2.17:68.4: But as to characteristic, a condition has the characteristic of assisting;
vsm2.17:68.5: for any given state that assists the presence or arising of a given state is called the latter’s condition.
vsm2.17:68.6: The words condition, cause, reason, source, originator, producer, etc., are one in meaning though different in the letter.
vsm2.17:68.7:
So, since it is a cause in the sense of a root, and a condition in the sense of assistance,
briefly a state that is assistantial in the sense of a root is a root-cause condition.
vsm2.17:69.1:
The intention of some teachers is that it establishes the profitable, etc., state in what
is profitable, etc., as paddy seeds, etc., do for paddy, etc.,
vsm2.17:69.2: and as the colour of gems, etc., do for the lustre of gems, and so on.
vsm2.17:69.3:
But if that is so, then it follows that the state of root-cause condition does
not apply to the kinds of materiality originated by it,
vsm2.17:69.4: for it does not establish any profitableness, etc., in them. Nevertheless, it is a condition for them,
vsm2.17:69.5:
for this is said: “Root-causes are a condition, as root-cause condition, for the states
associated with a root-cause and for the kinds of materiality originated thereby” (Paṭṭh I 1).
vsm2.17:69.6: Again, the indeterminateness of root-causeless consciousness is established without it.
vsm2.17:69.7: And the profitableness, etc., of those with root-cause is bound up with wise attention, etc., not with the associated root-causes.
vsm2.17:69.8: And if the profitableness, etc., resided in the associated root-causes as an individual essence,
vsm2.17:69.9:
then either the non-greed bound up with the root-cause in the associated states would
be only profitable or it would be only indeterminate;
vsm2.17:69.10:
but since it can be both, profitableness, etc., in the root-causes must still be sought for, just
as in the associated states such as wise attention, and so on.
vsm2.17:70.1:
70. But when the root-causes’ sense of root is taken as establishing stableness,
rather than as establishing profitableness, etc., there is no contradiction.
vsm2.17:70.2:
For states that have obtained a root-cause condition are firm, like trees, and stable; but those without
root-cause are, like moss with roots no bigger than sesame seeds, etc., unstable.
vsm2.17:70.3:
So an assistantial state may be understood as a root-cause condition, since it establishes
stableness through being of assistance in the sense of a root.
vsm2.17:71.1: 71. (2) As to the others that follow, a state that assists by being an object is an object condition.
vsm2.17:71.2:
Now, there are no states that are not object conditions; for the passage beginning “The visible-data base
is a condition, as object condition, for the eye-consciousness element” concludes thus:
vsm2.17:71.3:
“When any states, as states of consciousness and consciousness-concomitants, arise contingent upon any states,
these latter states are conditions, as object condition, for those former states” (Paṭṭh I 1).
vsm2.17:71.4: For just as a weak man both gets up and stands by hanging on to (ālambitvā) a stick or rope,
vsm2.17:71.5:
so states of consciousness and consciousness-concomitants always arise and are present
contingent upon visible data, etc., as their object (ārammaṇa = ālambana).
vsm2.17:71.6: Therefore all states that are objects of consciousness and consciousness-concomitants should be understood as object condition.
vsm2.17:72.1:
72. (3) A state that assists in the sense of being foremost is a predominance condition.
It is of two kinds as conascent and as object.
vsm2.17:72.2:
Herein, because of the passage beginning “Predominance of zeal is a condition, as predominance condition, for states
associated with zeal and for the kinds of materiality originated thereby” (Paṭṭh I 2),
vsm2.17:72.3:
it is the four states called zeal, purity of consciousness, energy, and inquiry,
that should be understood as predominance condition; but not simultaneously,
vsm2.17:72.4:
for when consciousness occurs with emphasis on zeal and putting zeal foremost,
then it is zeal and not the others that is predominant.
vsm2.17:72.6: But the state, by giving importance to which, immaterial states occur, is their object-predominance.
vsm2.17:72.7:
Hence it is said: “When any states, as states of consciousness and consciousness-concomitants,
arise by giving importance to any states,
vsm2.17:72.8: these latter states are a condition, as predominance condition, for those former states” (Paṭṭh I 2).
vsm2.17:73.1: 73. (4), (5) A state that assists by being proximate is a proximity condition.
vsm2.17:73.2: A state that assists by being contiguous is a contiguity condition.
vsm2.17:73.3: The explanation of this pair of conditions is very diffuse,
vsm2.17:73.4:
but substantially it is this: the regular order of consciousness begins thus, mind element is proximate (next)
after eye-consciousness, mind-consciousness element is proximate (next) after mind element,
vsm2.17:73.5:
and this is established only by each preceding consciousness, not otherwise; consequently, a state that is capable of arousing
an appropriate kind of consciousness proximate (next) to itself is a proximity condition.
vsm2.17:73.6:
Hence it is said: “Proximity condition: eye-consciousness and the states associated
therewith are a condition, as proximity condition,
vsm2.17:73.7: for mind element and for the states associated therewith” (Paṭṭh I 2).
vsm2.17:74.1: 74. (5) Proximity condition is the same as contiguity condition.
vsm2.17:74.2:
The difference here is only in the letter, there is none in the meaning; just as in the case of the words “growth” and “continuity”
(XIV.66), etc., and as in the case of the “terminology dyad,” “language dyad,” (Dhs §1306) and so on.
vsm2.17:74.3: There is no difference as to the sense.
vsm2.17:75.1:
75. The opinion of certain teachers is that proximity condition refers to proximity of aim
(fruit) and contiguity condition refers to proximity of time.
vsm2.17:75.2:
But that is contradicted by such statements as “The profitable consciousness belonging to the base
consisting of neither perception nor non-perception in one who emerges from cessation is a condition,
as contiguity condition, for fruition attainment consciousness” (Paṭṭh I 160).
vsm2.17:76.1:
76. Now, they say in this context that “the ability of states to produce their fruit
is not diminished, but the influence of meditative development prevents states from arising in proximity.”
vsm2.17:76.2: But that only establishes that there is no proximity of time;
vsm2.17:76.3: and we also say the same, namely, that there is no proximity of time there owing to the influence of development.
vsm2.17:76.4: But since there is no proximity of time, the state of contiguity condition is therefore impossible according to them
vsm2.17:76.5: since their belief is that the contiguity condition depends on proximity of time (cf. M-a II 363).
vsm2.17:76.6: Instead of adopting any such misinterpretation, the difference should be treated as residing in the letter only, not in the meaning.
vsm2.17:76.8: There is no interval (antara) between them, thus they are proximate (anantara);
vsm2.17:76.9: they are quite without interval because even the distinction of co-presence is lacking, thus they are contiguous (samanantara).
